headline_en: Taken to Nepal on promise of Australia and tortured; Sakib returns home after 8 months
summary_en: A van driver in Bagharpara, Jashore paid a broker 15 lakh taka to send his son Sakib Hossain to Australia, but the son was flown to Kathmandu, Nepal on 14 September 2025, locked up, beaten daily and used to extort more money. After about eight months he was pushed back into Bangladesh through India across the Nilphamari border and reached home on the night of Saturday 2 May 2026. A human trafficking case filed on 16 February 2026 names two men from the same village, who are absconding.

facts.statement: Van driver Alamgir Hossain (44) of Kismat Mahmudpur village, Bagharpara upazila, Jashore handed 15 lakh taka to a broker to send his son Sakib Hossain (21) to Australia.

Sakib Hossain was told he was flying to Australia but on 14 September 2025 was taken to Kathmandu, Nepal instead; he only realised after the plane landed that he was at Kathmandu airport. The family lost contact with him some days later.

At Dhaka airport Sakib was in a group of five, one of whom was the broker's man, and the broker's man held the passports. At Kathmandu airport he got his passport back to clear immigration, and once outside the airport the broker's man took his passport and the dollars he carried worth 80,000 taka.

Outside Kathmandu airport the broker's man told Sakib that the Australia flight was in two days and that two Bengalis would collect him, then left; after about two and a half hours two men came, took his mobile phone and took him to 'North Bengal Hotel' in Nepal.

Sakib was kept in a three-bed room of the hotel with three people staying in it, was not allowed outside, and was locked in from outside whenever the broker's men went out. He was beaten every day for money.

When Sakib's family called, the captors gave him the phone and made him say what they dictated while sitting beside him with a knife, threatening him if he deviated. They demanded a further 1.5 lakh taka and kept beating him even after taking that money.

After four months in the hotel, two new men took Sakib by taxi to an empty house in a deserted place in Nepal and kept him in a basement room with little light or air; he was first given rice three days after arriving, was beaten daily (also when he asked for rice), and during one beating was slashed in the abdomen with a knife and badly injured. He was not beaten in the last 15 days.

Return route described by Sakib: on Thursday night two captors took him by bus from Nepal to Siliguri, India, changed bus and reached Jalpaiguri the next noon, then by auto to a place where he was handed over; one man walked him to an empty field, another walked him across a nearly dry river, and late Friday night he was passed under the barbed wire through a culvert and pushed into Bangladesh across the Nilphamari border. He reached home by train on Saturday night (about 2 May 2026).

Alamgir Hossain filed a case on 16 February 2026 at the Human Trafficking and Migrant Smuggling Prevention and Suppression Tribunal-1, Jashore; on the court's order the Bagharpara police station OC recorded it as an FIR. The accused are Tarikul Islam (45), son of Mokles Mollya of Kismat Mahmudpur village, and Nazmul Hossain (35).

Investigating officer SI Gobinda Kumar Mondal of Bagharpara police station said the accused in the Sakib Hossain trafficking case are absconding and cannot be found, and efforts to arrest them continue.
facts.source_in_article: SI Gobinda Kumar Mondal, Bagharpara police station

facts.statement: To raise the money Alamgir Hossain sold all his land except the homestead (he had 22 decimals: 14 decimals homestead and 8 decimals litchi orchard), sold his engine-driven van, his only source of income, and borrowed 12.5 lakh taka from five NGOs and samitis; creditors now sit at his house every day.
Prothom Alo online had reported Sakib's disappearance in Nepal on 16 April 2026 under the headline 'Taken to Nepal on the promise of Australia, parents cannot find the young man'.

headline_en: Young man missing on the way to Italy; no trace even after paying 43 lakh taka
summary_en: Alvi Khan (24) of Madaripur Sadar, who set out for Italy irregularly through a local broker, has been missing in Libya for 19 days as of 22 April 2026. His family paid the 21 lakh taka contract price and then 22 lakh taka in ransom after he was held in a Libyan detention house. The broker Ratul Hawlader was arrested after a human trafficking case filed on 19 April.

facts.statement: The broker ring contracted to deliver Alvi Khan (24) of Kuntipara village, Ghatmajhi union, Madaripur Sadar to Italy for 21 lakh taka; the family paid one third of it on 15 October 2025 under the contract.

On 19 October 2025, four days after the first payment, members of the broker ring flew Alvi Khan to Saudi Arabia; from there a Bangladeshi broker ring living in Libya took him to a detention house (bondishala) in Libya.

According to the family, Alvi was held in Libya for the first three months without torture while the full contract money was extracted by trickery; four months after the money was taken he was tortured and audio voice messages were sent to the family demanding ransom. (The article also dates the ransom payment to 4 November, which does not fit this timeline.)

Alvi Khan's family paid 22 lakh taka in ransom on 4 November through various banks; his mother said this 22 lakh was given to broker Ratul and that 21 lakh had been taken before. When more ransom was demanded the family refused. The headline gives the total as 43 lakh taka.
As of 22 April 2026 Alvi Khan had been missing from Libya for 19 days with no contact; his last message was a voice note telling his mother to have his father pay or 'they will kill me'.
facts.source_in_article: mother Merina Begum, father Emdad Hossain

facts.statement: Alvi's father Emdad Hossain filed a case on 19 April 2026 under the human trafficking suppression law at Madaripur Sadar Model Police Station against six named people including Ratul; police arrested the main accused Ratul Hawlader, who is in Madaripur jail, and are looking for the others.
facts.source_in_article: article; OC Abul Kalam Azad, Madaripur Sadar Model Police Station

facts.statement: Ratul Hawlader (28), son of Sarwar Hawlader of Dhulgram, Baligram union, Dasar upazila, Madaripur, is described as long involved in a human trafficking ring that first earned a reputation by getting over a hundred youths from Dasar and Sadar upazilas to Italy by boat from the Libyan coast, then lured youths to Libya, held them in detention houses and collected ransom from within Bangladesh.

Ratul's father Sarwar Hawlader, who says he is also an accused in the same case, denied that Ratul held Alvi for money and said Ratul 'works as an agency for various countries' and does nothing illegal.

headline_en: Eastern and Central Europe: the unfamiliar corridor of Bangladeshi migration
summary_en: An opinion column by two academics describes growing Bangladeshi migration to Central and Eastern Europe (Poland, Romania, Bulgaria, Hungary, Czech Republic) as students and as workers in construction, manufacturing, agriculture, logistics and services. It lists the obstacles: weak recruitment regulation at home, skill gaps, few Bangladeshi embassies there and few European embassies in Dhaka, unsubsidised costs, thin community networks and anti-migrant sentiment, and urges better governance, diplomacy and training.

facts.statement: The number of Bangladeshis legally staying in Poland rose from 160 in 2014 to more than 6,000 in 2025, according to the column's authors.
facts.source_in_article: column authors Dr Anas Ansar and Dr Zbynek Mucha

facts.statement: The columnists say ageing populations, growing labour markets and worker shortages in Central and Eastern European countries such as Poland, Romania, Bulgaria, Hungary and the Czech Republic are attracting Asian migrants, and Bangladeshis, Nepalis and Indians have become a visible group filling the gap; they expect demand for foreign workers to continue because the shortage is structural (ageing and local workers leaving for Western Europe).

According to the column, some Bangladeshis go to Central and Eastern Europe as university students because tuition is comparatively low and the visa process easier than in many Western European countries; others work in construction, manufacturing, agriculture, logistics and services where shortages are acute; many treat the region as a stepping stone to richer European countries.

The column states Bangladesh has no embassy in several Central and Eastern European countries including the Czech Republic and Romania, so consular services there are often provided on a temporary or limited basis.

The column states that only nine of the European Union's '29' countries (figure as printed) have a diplomatic or consular presence in Bangladesh, and most European embassies are located in India, which makes it hard for prospective migrants to get correct information and visa or other consular help.

The columnists warn that labour migration to Central and Eastern Europe, unlike Gulf migration, is generally not subsidised so the whole process needs more personal investment; the corridor is new so there are very few established Bangladeshi communities or networks to rely on; and many Bangladeshi migrants lack the specific technical skills these labour markets need, which can push them into precarious or low-paid work.

The columnists say weak institutional coordination and inadequate control of recruitment in Bangladesh force many migrants to new destinations to rely on informal or poorly regulated recruitment channels, raising risk and cost.

The column says anti-immigration rhetoric remains strong in some Central and Eastern European countries, migrants from Muslim-majority countries sometimes face suspicion or discrimination, and there have been cases of Bangladeshi entrepreneurs facing police surveillance under broad 'security' or counter-terrorism measures.
The column states that Bangladesh has become a major source country of irregular migration to Europe and that Bangladeshi citizens have repeatedly died crossing the Mediterranean recently.

The column says the corridor began in the 1970s and 1980s when socialist states such as then Czechoslovakia, Poland and Belarus gave scholarships to Bangladeshi students; a small number stayed on and became the pioneers of the Bangladeshi community in the region.

headline_en: Meeting on opening Malaysia's labour market; emphasis on cutting costs
summary_en: Bangladesh and Malaysia held a bilateral labour migration meeting in Putrajaya on Thursday 9 April 2026 and agreed to speed up reopening the closed Malaysian labour market to Bangladeshi workers based on sector-wise demand, with a fair, ethical and transparent recruitment process. A joint statement promises fewer intermediaries, credible recruiting agencies, fast completion of recruitment of stuck workers, and a Malaysian AI-based recruitment system intended to bring worker cost to zero.

facts.statement: As of 9 April 2026 the Malaysian labour market was closed to Bangladeshi workers; at a bilateral meeting in Putrajaya that day the two governments agreed to speed up the process of reopening it based on Malaysia's sector-wise demand and to ensure a fair, ethical and transparent recruitment process.
facts.source_in_article: Mahdi Amin, adviser to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman

facts.statement: The Bangladesh-Malaysia joint press statement of 9 April 2026 says steps will be taken to cut migration cost by reducing intermediaries, to use credible recruiting agencies, and to quickly complete the recruitment of workers who are stuck.

The joint statement says Malaysia has taken an initiative to introduce an AI-based, technology-driven recruitment system for all source countries, which is to reduce middlemen and migration cost and make the cost to workers zero, in line with the ILO-guided 'employer pays' principle; Bangladesh expressed full support for implementing such a digital platform as a global initiative involving all sending countries.

The two sides discussed concerns about ongoing human trafficking legal cases; Bangladesh reaffirmed its commitment to rule of law, due process, accountability and timely justice. They also exchanged views on irregular workers' problems, skills development, training, certification and information sharing.

Bangladesh's Minister for Labour and Employment and for Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Ariful Haque Chowdhury and PM's adviser Mahdi Amin went to Malaysia on Wednesday 8 April 2026, the first visit to discuss the labour market since the new Bangladesh government took office; the Malaysian side at the meeting was led by Human Resources Minister Dato' Sri Ramanan Ramakrishnan, and the minister also met Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim at his office on 9 April.

A press release said the two countries reaffirmed a joint commitment to a transparent, clean and effective recruitment system to prevent exploitation of workers, and also discussed trade, investment, teacher exchange and cooperation in education.

headline_en: Seven rescued during attempt to traffic them to Malaysia by sea
summary_en: The Coast Guard rescued seven people including women and children on Monday 30 March 2026 from a house in Dakshin Lombori, Teknaf, Cox's Bazar that it says was a traffickers' den. They had been lured with promises of a better life, high-paid jobs and cheap passage and were to be taken to Malaysia by sea; the traffickers fled.

facts.statement: On the afternoon of Monday 30 March 2026 the Coast Guard raided a dwelling house in the Dakshin Lombori area of Teknaf, Cox's Bazar, which it says is a human traffickers' den, and rescued seven people including women and children who had been brought there to be trafficked to Malaysia by sea. The traffickers sensed the raid and fled; the seven were handed to Teknaf Model Police Station.
facts.source_in_article: Coast Guard media officer Lt Commander Sabbir Alam

facts.statement: According to the Coast Guard's preliminary questioning, an organised trafficking ring brought the seven to the Teknaf den by offering the dream of a better life abroad, high-paid jobs and taking them abroad at low cost, planning to take them to Malaysia by sea.

headline_en: Masud Uddin Chowdhury remanded in the very case in which CID had filed a final report
summary_en: Dhaka's Detective Branch (DB) arrested retired Lt Gen Masud Uddin Chowdhury on Monday 23 March 2026 and took him on five-day remand in a Paltan police station human trafficking case over the Malaysia labour-export syndicate, a case that CID had earlier closed as 'false' in a final report. The complainant, a recruiting-firm owner, objected, the court ordered DB to reinvestigate, and one accused gave a confessional statement in December 2025. The rest of the article recounts Masud Uddin's role in the 2007 '1/11' changeover.

facts.statement: On 3 September 2024, after the fall of the Awami League government, Altab Khan, owner of a firm named Afia Overseas, filed a case under the human trafficking law at Paltan police station, Dhaka against 103 accused over labour export to Malaysia. The accused include former expatriates' welfare minister Imran Ahmed, former senior secretary of the expatriates' welfare ministry Ahmed Munirus Salehin, former Feni MP Nizam Hazari, former Dhaka-20 MP Benzir Ahmed, and retired Lt Gen Masud Uddin Chowdhury (accused no. 3, former Feni-3 MP).
facts.source_in_article: case documents reviewed by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: The Paltan Malaysia-syndicate trafficking case was first investigated by Paltan police, then moved to CID, which on 15 July 2025 filed a final report in court saying the case was false and recommending action against the complainant for filing a false case. The complainant filed a no-confidence (naraji) petition and the court ordered DB to reinvestigate.

DB arrested Masud Uddin Chowdhury on Monday (about 23 March 2026) from his home in Baridhara DOHS, Dhaka, showed him arrested in the Paltan trafficking case and took him on five days' remand through the court on Tuesday.

DMP Detective Branch Joint Commissioner Mohammad Nasirul Islam said a ring (chokro) was built around manpower export to Malaysia during the previous government and Masud Uddin Chowdhury was a powerful member of it; he is being questioned about the ring and the source of his power.
facts.source_in_article: Mohammad Nasirul Islam, Joint Commissioner, DMP DB

facts.statement: In December 2025 accused no. 12 in the case, S M Rafiq, gave a confessional statement in court; a DB officer said it contains information that human trafficking and embezzlement of a huge amount of money took place in the name of manpower export to Malaysia.

CID supervising officer Additional Special SP Mostafizur Rahman said that when CID got the case 76 of the 103 accused were on bail and the rest absconding, so they could not be questioned, and the complainant could not produce enough evidence; a Penal Code extortion section of the case also got a final report, which the court accepted. He said the complainant was told the results; the complainant says he was not and alleges CID compromised with the accused.

headline_en: 'I beg at your feet, bring back my son's body'
summary_en: Munna Talukdar (19) of Rajoir, Madaripur left home on 12 October 2025 for Italy under a 22.5 lakh taka 'body contract' with local brokers, was moved through Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Egypt and Benghazi to Misrata, Libya, and was put on a boat on 1 November that was attacked at sea; he and another Rajoir youth were shot dead. The family learned of the death on 18 November, the body's whereabouts are unknown, and police say they will act if families file a complaint.

facts.statement: The family of Munna Talukdar (19) of Purba Durgabardi, Badarpasha union, Rajoir upazila, Madaripur contracted with brokers for 22.5 lakh taka to get him to Italy; his mother Rabeya Begum said the broker took him on a 'body contract', promising to get him to Italy by any means, and fled with the 22.5 lakh taka.
facts.source_in_article: family and local sources; mother Rabeya Begum

facts.statement: Route described for Munna Talukdar: left home 12 October 2025; taken from Bangladesh to Saudi Arabia, where he performed Umrah; then to Kuwait for a few days; then Egypt; then by plane to Benghazi, Libya; then to Misrata, Libya; on 1 November put on an engine boat from the Libyan coast towards Italy with other migrants.

Shortly after the boat carrying Munna Talukdar set out into the Mediterranean from Libya it was attacked by 'mafia' (pirates); Munna (19) and Bayezid Sheikh (18) of Ghoshalkandi, Badarpasha union, Rajoir, Madaripur were shot dead. Three people from Madaripur district were shot dead in Libya in this incident per police and the article, all under broker Shipon Khan.
facts.source_in_article: family and local sources; reporter's inquiry

facts.statement: Munna's relatives repeatedly went to the broker's house for news and the broker finally told the family of his death on 18 November 2025, more than two weeks after the boat left; nobody can say where the body is.

Local brokers Nannu and Manju of Badarpasha village, Rajoir work for Shipon Khan, a Bangladeshi broker living in Libya described as a leading member of a human trafficking ring, whose village home is in Adityapur, Kunia union, Madaripur Sadar; his aunt Setara Begum said Shipon himself left for Italy, now lives in Libya and 'has taken many more people'.
At Misrata, Libya the broker assured Munna's family that their son would have no problem and 'not even a flower's touch would fall on him' before putting him on the boat.

Madaripur Additional Superintendent of Police (Crime and Investigation) Jahangir Alam said police learned from social media of three people shot dead in Libya and will take legal action against the brokers if the victim families file a complaint or case; the father said no broker had been tried so far.
Before leaving, Munna Talukdar worked as a house painter in Dhaka and his father is a farmer; the family lives in a broken tin-shed house.

headline_en: Over a hundred missing in boat sinking near Malaysia-Thailand border; 13 recovered including a Bangladeshi
summary_en: A boat carrying migrants that started from Buthidaung, Myanmar with about 300 people sank near Thai-Malaysian waters; by Sunday 9 November 2025 Malaysia's maritime agency MMEA had found 12 survivors and one body near Langkawi, with over a hundred missing. One survivor is Bangladeshi. Passengers had been split into three smaller boats of about 100 each to evade Malaysian authorities.

facts.statement: A boat with migrants sank near the Thailand-Malaysia maritime boundary about three days before 9 November 2025; by Sunday 9 November 12 people were rescued alive and one body (a Rohingya woman) recovered from waters near Langkawi island, and more than a hundred were missing. The survivors include one Bangladeshi, two Rohingya and three Myanmar nationals (as listed by Kedah police via Bernama).
facts.source_in_article: MMEA; Kedah police chief Adzli Abu Shah via Bernama; First Admiral Romli Mustafa

facts.statement: Kedah police chief Adzli Abu Shah said the vessel left Buthidaung, Myanmar with about 300 people; near the Malaysian coast the passengers were split into three smaller boats of about 100 each, a tactic taught by those who arranged the boats to evade Malaysian authorities. One boat sank and the position of the other two was unknown.
facts.source_in_article: Kedah police chief Adzli Abu Shah

facts.statement: AFP, citing Malaysian media, reported that Rohingya who try to reach Malaysia or other Southeast Asian countries by sea through syndicates pay 3 lakh 52 thousand to 3 lakh 85 thousand taka each (USD 3,200 to 3,500, as printed).

headline_en: Sending workers to new countries will be possible within three years
summary_en: A short first-person piece by Expatriates' Welfare adviser Professor Asif Nazrul (published 20 August 2025). He says unskilled labour demand in the Middle East is falling, that Bangladesh is targeting Japan, Korea and Europe for skilled workers, that Malaysia sending would start in about a month, that the UAE remains complicated and Oman is regularising irregular workers, and lists airport measures for migrants.

facts.statement: Expatriates' Welfare adviser Asif Nazrul wrote on 20 August 2025 that after bilateral talks on closed labour markets, sending workers to Malaysia would begin within about a month.
facts.source_in_article: Asif Nazrul, adviser, Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment

facts.statement: Asif Nazrul said the UAE labour market is 'a bit complicated': expatriates who took part there in the July mass uprising protests are law-breakers in the UAE's eyes, and this still has some negative effect there.
Asif Nazrul said that after talks with Oman's minister, Oman is regularising irregular workers, and he hoped new worker recruitment to Oman would become possible during the interim government's term.

Asif Nazrul said that if things proceed properly more than one lakh (100,000) workers can be sent to Japan in the next five years, and that Bangladesh is trying to send skilled workers to Japan, Korea and Europe.

Asif Nazrul said demand for unskilled labour in the Middle East is falling fast with technology; even loading-unloading or construction work now needs some skill, and the ministry is trying to build that skill for the Middle East.

Asif Nazrul listed steps taken for migrants at the airport: an expatriates' lounge (probashi lounge), round-the-clock helpers, and a place to stay overnight; he said he is also working on a hospital owned by expatriates but does not know how far it will get.

Asif Nazrul said the government does no official labour-market research to explore markets and Bangladesh's missions abroad do no notable work on it; he hoped that within three years skilled, semi-skilled, seasonal and permanent workers could be sent to new countries, and said a to-do document would be left for the next government.

headline_en: What effect could the Iran-Israel war have on Bangladesh's economy
summary_en: An economic analysis (17 June 2025) of how an Iran-Israel war could hit Bangladesh through fuel prices, LNG supply via the Strait of Hormuz, inflation, trade and aviation. On migration it says few Bangladeshi workers are in Iran or Israel, but a regional spread could cost jobs, stop or cut new hiring in Middle East countries, disrupt flights and reduce remittances; Oman, beside the Strait of Hormuz, is Bangladesh's sixth largest remittance source.

facts.statement: By May 2025 figures, Iran is not among Bangladesh's top 30 remittance source countries, while Oman, next to the Strait of Hormuz, is Bangladesh's sixth largest source of remittances.

The analysis says there are hardly any Bangladeshi migrant workers in Iran or Israel, so they would not be directly affected by the June 2025 Iran-Israel war, but if the war spread regionally Middle East construction, services and housing sectors could stall, workers could suddenly lose jobs, and countries could stop or cut new recruitment.

The analysis says that in a war situation flight cancellations or limits would disrupt workers' travel and could raise costs; civil aviation sector people said only a handful of Bangladesh's flights use Iranian airspace, so the effect would be small, a ticket price rise is unlikely and only schedules would need changing, as happened during the three-day India-Pakistan war in May 2025.
The article notes that in earlier Middle East wars Bangladeshi workers were forced to return home.

Dhaka University economics teacher Selim Raihan said the war situation could cause multiple negative effects on Bangladesh's economy, including fuel-price inflation, higher trade costs and lower remittances.

headline_en: Coordinated initiative urgent to protect migrant women's rights
summary_en: At a BRAC Migration Programme workshop in Dhaka on Wednesday 7 May 2025, government and NGO representatives said women migrants face sexual harassment, abuse and wage discrimination abroad and need coordinated support on return. Speakers gave figures on women abroad and returnees, and BRAC's 'Network for Bangladeshi Women Migrants' was presented as a platform through which agencies will offer services to returnee women.

facts.statement: According to BMET data cited in the article, Bangladesh ranks sixth among migrant-sending countries; more than one crore (10 million) Bangladeshis are abroad as migrants, about 10 lakh (1 million) of them women, and most Bangladeshi women migrants work as domestic workers in Middle East countries.
facts.source_in_article: BMET data as cited by the article

facts.statement: BRAC associate director (Migration and Youth Platform) Shariful Hasan said more than 67,000 women were forced to return to Bangladesh in the past six years after falling into various crises abroad, many of them victims of abuse.

A T M Mahbub-ul-Karim, joint secretary of the expatriates' welfare ministry and director of the Wage Earners' Welfare Board's RAISE project, said the government has identified and served about 31,000 returnee women, and the work is continuing.

SME Foundation chairperson Md Mushfiqur Rahman said the SME Foundation will work on making returnee women into entrepreneurs, with training and financial support; he said most people who return from abroad have no skills.

BRAC's 'Network for Bangladeshi Women Migrants' (chairperson Sheepa Hafiza), set up to support returnee Bangladeshi women, is to bring government and non-government bodies together to offer their services to returnee women; the workshop was held under the EU-BRAC project 'Improved Sustainable Reintegration of Bangladeshi Returnee Migrants'.

Md Saiful Haque Chowdhury, additional secretary (planning and development) of the expatriates' welfare ministry, said the government is working to improve services for returnee women in all areas starting from service at the airport.

Manusher Jonno Foundation executive director Shaheen Anam asked why unskilled women workers are sent at all, saying unskilled women abroad cannot negotiate or bargain over pay; BAIRA secretary general Ali Haider Chowdhury said countries like the Philippines act immediately when their women migrants have problems and that abusive employers must be blacklisted.

The article states that for lack of proper monitoring by authorities many Bangladeshi women who go abroad face sexual harassment, abuse and wage discrimination; a linked headline notes women worker departures have been falling for two years.

headline_en: Japan to take more workers at no cost; MoU signed
summary_en: On Thursday 10 April 2025 the expatriates' welfare ministry signed an MoU with Japanese private company Onodera User Run Incorporation under which Bangladeshi workers get free Japanese language and technical training and then jobs in Japan at no migration cost. The article also describes the existing IM Japan technical intern route (since 2017): four months of language training at BMET centres, an exam, four more months under IM Japan, then placement, with stated pay ranges.

facts.statement: On 10 April 2025 the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment signed an MoU with Japanese private company Onodera User Run Incorporation (signed by senior secretary Neyamat Ullah Bhuiyan and vice president Takashi Sugeno): Bangladeshi workers are to get free Japanese language and technical training, and trained workers are to get jobs in Japan with no migration cost.
Under the Onodera User Run MoU, training is to be offered in the caregiver, industrial packaging, plastic moulding, rod binding, scaffolding, car painting, welding and automobile mechanic trades.
Adviser Asif Nazrul said 695 technical interns went from Bangladesh to Japan in the past seven years; workers have been going to Japan as technical interns since 2017.

Existing government route to Japan: under a 2017 MoU between the ministry and International Manpower Development Organization (IM) Japan, BMET gives Japanese language training at technical training centres in various districts; after the four-month language course workers sit an exam, those who pass get four more months of training managed by IM Japan, and are then taken to Japan as technical interns.
Workers sent to Japan as technical interns under the IM Japan route are paid the equivalent of BDT 124,500 to BDT 157,700 (the article does not state the pay period).

The article states there is no way to go to Japan for work without learning Japanese, and that Japan is conservative about taking foreign workers; work opportunities exist in construction, technology, nursing, agriculture, and hotel management and tourism, and in care of the elderly.
The article states that going to Japan through Japanese language training is possible at no cost (bina khoroche).

headline_en: 'Ami Probashi' annual report: number of workers going abroad fell 27% in 2024
summary_en: The 2024 annual report of the digital migration platform 'Ami Probashi' says 1,009,146 Bangladeshi workers went abroad in 2024, down 27 percent from 1,390,811 in 2023. Saudi Arabia took 62 percent; Malaysia, the second largest destination, fell to 93,000 because of its new labour policy. BMET registrations rose and women's share of registrations rose from 2.78 to 4.79 percent, while technical training centre enrolment roughly halved.

facts.statement: A total of 1,009,146 Bangladeshi workers went abroad in 2024, 27 percent fewer than the 1,390,811 who went in 2023, according to the 'Ami Probashi' Annual Report 2024.

Saudi Arabia was the top destination for Bangladeshi workers in 2024 as in the previous year, taking 62 percent of all workers; the report says the country has demand for skilled and unskilled workers in infrastructure construction and other sectors.

Malaysia was the second largest destination for Bangladeshi workers in 2024 with 93,000 workers going, a significant fall; the Ami Probashi report says Malaysia's new labour policy is the main reason for the drop.
Enrolment in technical training centre courses fell to 112,166 in 2024 from 236,270 the previous year, according to the Ami Probashi report.

Total BMET registrations were 798,276 in 2024 against 660,088 in 2023; women's share of BMET registrations rose from 2.78 percent in 2023 to 4.79 percent in 2024 (the report describes women's participation as more than doubling).
The Ami Probashi report says economic instability from the July-August 2024 mass uprising and political changeover put outbound workers in some uncertainty and contributed to the fall in migration.
'Ami Probashi' is described as a digital migration platform; its founder and managing director is Tariq E Haque.

headline_en: Why expatriates are still ignored even after the mass uprising
summary_en: An opinion column by migration scholar Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder (14 January 2025) argues that Bangladeshi political parties' reform plans (BNP's 31 points, Jamaat's 41 points) omit migration and diaspora issues despite migrants' remittances and their role in the July-August 2024 uprising. It cites remittance figures, hundi reliance, high recruitment costs and abuse abroad, and proposes manifesto commitments, stronger bilateral agreements, a migration task force and a capable minister.

facts.statement: The columnist states that migrant workers send more than USD 21 billion in remittances a year, contributing more than 6 percent of Bangladesh's GDP, and that migration directly affects the lives of more than four crore (40 million) people in Bangladesh.
The columnist says migrant workers and the diaspora stopped sending remittances for a time and organised protests worldwide in support of the July-August 2024 student-people's uprising.

The columnist says over-reliance on informal systems such as hundi diverts several billion dollars away from formal banking channels, and that unregulated recruitment drives up costs for migrant workers and puts many families in a debt cycle; Bangladesh is also over-dependent on a few destination countries.

The columnist says migrant workers abroad often work long hours for low pay and live in poor housing, and women workers in particular face exploitation and abuse, with no strong policy protecting their rights.

The columnist notes BNP's 31-point and Jamaat-e-Islami's 41-point state reform plans do not include migration or diaspora issues, and proposes that parties commit to stronger bilateral agreements with labour-receiving countries (fair wages, safe workplaces, legal protection), legal aid for exploited migrants, a migration task force, and a capable expatriates' welfare minister.

The column cites the Philippines' Overseas Workers Welfare Administration (financial aid, training, rehabilitation for overseas workers) and 'Balik Scientist Program', India's Pravasi Bharatiya Divas and Overseas Citizen of India scheme, and Tunisia's post-2011 migrant-rights policies as models.

headline_en: How expatriates can be engaged to counter disinformation
summary_en: An opinion column by Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder (19 December 2024) on engaging Bangladeshi diaspora and migrant workers, through embassies, training and platforms, to counter disinformation about Bangladesh. Its migration-relevant content is on remittances: the chief adviser urged migrants to send more money through legal channels, and the columnist claims USD 10-12 billion a year moves through hundi and urges awareness campaigns for legal channels.

facts.statement: The columnist states that USD 10-12 billion leaves Bangladesh every year through hundi, and claims this money is used for illegal drugs, human trafficking, gold smuggling and disinformation in India and Myanmar.

The columnist urges the government and Bangladeshi embassies to run large awareness programmes telling migrant workers to stop sending money by hundi and use legal channels; interim government chief adviser Muhammad Yunus, in his first address to the nation, called on expatriates to send more remittances through legal channels.

The columnist says many migrant workers are illiterate or semi-educated, cannot verify information and fall into disinformation and hate traps, and proposes that embassies run simple-language training, a central information repository on social media, and regular discussions and workshops with migrant communities.

headline_en: Where are the 18 young men? Families have not known for 9 months
summary_en: Eighteen young men from villages of Angaria union, Shariatpur Sadar left in 2022 and 2023 to reach Italy irregularly through Libya via broker Rashed Khan, paying 12 to 20 lakh taka each. Several were jailed or held for ransom in Libya, and families have had no contact with any of them since 21-22 March 2024. Families formed a human chain at the Deputy Commissioner's office on Sunday 8 December 2024; the broker has fled and police say they will start a shadow investigation.

facts.statement: Relatives say Rashed Khan of Char Jadabpur village, Angaria union, Shariatpur Sadar collects people from various areas of Shariatpur through two associates and sends them to various countries; he has a firm named Lamisa Enterprise and an office in Paltan, Dhaka. In 2022 and 2023 he took 18 young men from home to send them irregularly to Italy via Libya. He has locked his village home and fled with relatives, his Paltan office is closed, and his cousin Abdur Rahman Khan says he is hiding inside Bangladesh.
facts.source_in_article: relatives of the missing; reporter's visit; cousin Abdur Rahman Khan

facts.statement: The broker took between 12 and 20 lakh taka in various ways from each family of the 18 Shariatpur men sent towards Italy via Libya.

The 18 Shariatpur men were taken first to the United Arab Emirates, then Egypt, then Libya. Some were arrested twice by police in Libya and jailed; some were held hostage and tortured and freed after relatives paid.

Relatives have had no contact with any of the 18 men since 21 and 22 March 2024 (about nine months as of 8 December 2024); one wife said her husband told her on 22 March they were about to set off by sea from Libya to Italy.

Siraj Mridha (35), a farmer of Niyamatpur village, paid Rashed 5 lakh taka (on loans) and left in December 2022: taken to Dubai, then Egypt, then Benghazi, Libya. A Libyan ring then held him hostage and his wife Ayesha Akter sold the homestead with 6 decimals of land and sent the ring 8 lakh taka. He last phoned on 21 March 2024.

Al Amin Bhuiyan (25), an electrician of Dakshin Madhyapara, Shariatpur Sadar, paid Rashed 12.5 lakh taka and left in June 2023; his father Chunnu Bhuiyan sold 20 decimals of land. He was taken to Libya, arrested by police and spent 75 days in jail, then moved to Tripoli for the sea crossing to Italy; no contact since 22 March 2024.
When Al Amin's father asked the broker about his missing son he was told 'your son is fine, he will go to Italy soon'; the broker then absconded about three months before December 2024.

The families applied to the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment asking for the men to be traced (the article's opening says the application was to the Foreign Ministry and brought no result), formed a human chain at about 11 am on 8 December 2024 in front of the Shariatpur Deputy Commissioner's office and gave the DC a memorandum.

Shariatpur Superintendent of Police Nazrul Islam said he had scattered information that the 18 were victims of human trafficking; police can take legal steps if the families file a case, and would now begin a shadow investigation.

The 18 missing men named by relatives: Al Amin Bhuiyan (Dakshin Madhyapara), Didar Hossain and Mohammad Faruk Sardar (Dakshin Bhasanchar), Aldin Rimon (Notun Hat), Rashidul, Siraj and Atikur Rahman (Char Neyamatpur), Aminul Islam (Char Bhasanchar), Sardar Sadekul (Chapatoli), Miraj Ojha, Rafiq Moral and Shamim Gazi (Charchatang), Mohammad Parvez (Jagir), Zafar Sheikh (Darichar Dadpur), Dipu Sikder (Jafrabad), Shahjahan Hawlader (Tribhagadi), Shahin Sikder (Kadamtali) and Saiful Islam (Surjomoni), all of Shariatpur Sadar.

headline_en: Jordan to take 738 workers; pay from 21 thousand to 1 lakh 68 thousand taka
summary_en: A recruitment notice (published 2 October 2024): through the state-owned BOESL, several Jordanian apparel companies (Tusker Apparel, Classic Fashion, Jia Apparel) will hire 738 women and men, mostly women machine operators plus supervisors and executives. The notice gives pay per post, contract terms, which fees the employer covers, the documents to bring, and the interview date and place.

facts.statement: Through Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL), several apparel companies in Jordan are to recruit 738 women and men workers, per a notice reported on 2 October 2024.

BOESL Jordan notice, women machine operators (relevant experience required, age 20 to 35): Tusker Apparel Company 250 posts, Classic Fashion Company 300 posts, Jia Apparel Company 100 posts; monthly basic pay BDT 21,118 for each.

BOESL Jordan notice, Classic Fashion Company supervisory and executive posts with monthly basic pay: production supervisor 20 (women/men) BDT 59,132; quality supervisor 20 (men) BDT 59,132; production executive 10 (men) BDT 109,816; quality executive 10 (men) BDT 101,369; industrial engineer executive 10 (men) BDT 135,159; mechanical executive 5 (men) BDT 101,369; technical executive 10 (men) BDT 109,816; trade union representative 3 (women) BDT 135,159 to BDT 168,948. These posts need at least five years' experience in the field.

Terms in the BOESL Jordan garment notice: 8 hours' duty a day, 6 days a week, with overtime; contract of three years, renewable; the employer pays accommodation, food, primary medical care and transport, the joining air fare, and the return air fare after three years of satisfactory service; other terms follow Jordanian labour law.

Under the BOESL Jordan notice, anyone with a case against them in Bangladesh or Jordan is ineligible, and anyone holding more than one passport must bring them all. Returnees from Jordan or other countries are given priority on qualification and skill, as are certificate holders trained in the garments trade at BMET-run technical training centres.

For selected workers the recruiting company in Jordan bears BOESL's service charge, the departure (embarkation) tax, 15 percent VAT on the service charge, BOESL's registration fee, the smart card fee and the Wage Earners' welfare fee; the selected worker must pay the medical fee and the fingerprint fee.

headline_en: 70 percent of workers who could not go to Malaysia have got their money back: state minister
summary_en: The expatriates' welfare ministry had ordered recruiting agencies to refund within 15 days (by 18 July 2024) the workers who completed the process but could not fly to Malaysia. On Thursday 25 July 2024 State Minister Shafiqur Rahman Chowdhury said BAIRA reports 70 percent have been refunded, that exact numbers will be known once BAIRA submits a list, and that the reopening of the market may become clear at a joint technical committee meeting next month. He also said Bangladesh will not intervene for expatriates punished in the UAE for protesting.

facts.statement: The Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment instructed that workers who finalised the process but could not go to Malaysia be refunded within 15 days, which meant by 18 July 2024.

On 25 July 2024 the state minister said BAIRA had informed him that 70 percent of the workers who could not go to Malaysia had received refunds, but the exact number could not yet be stated: workers are to confirm in writing after receiving what they paid, and BAIRA is to submit that list to the ministry.
The state minister said legal action would be taken against recruiting agencies that fail to refund the full amount to workers who could not go to Malaysia.

Asked when the Malaysian labour market might reopen, the state minister said a letter had been sent to the Malaysian government about the workers who could not go, and that the Bangladesh-Malaysia joint technical committee would meet the following month (August 2024), when the reopening would become known.

On Bangladeshis punished in the UAE, the state minister said expatriates who protested in Dubai broke the law and were sentenced to various terms, that Bangladesh would not intervene on behalf of the convicted expatriates as it is that state's matter, and that workers should know the law of the country they live in.

It is collecting information from the immigration department, 101 recruiting agencies and BAIRA.

Malaysia closed its labour market under international pressure over widespread irregularities by a syndicate and set 31 May 2024 as the deadline for approved workers to enter; about 17,000 Bangladeshi workers who had completed all steps and held BMET clearance could not go.

The state minister said no one responsible would be spared, refunds would be discussed so that workers get maximum compensation, no syndicate would be accepted, the government wants all agencies to be able to work, and legal action would be taken against agencies whose workers got no work after reaching Malaysia.

An 11-member delegation from various Japanese companies, led by Masafumi Yurigami of Yurigami Maritime Company Limited (spelling as transliterated from Bangla), met the state minister on 9 June 2024; several Japanese private firms proposed taking more skilled workers from Bangladesh, particularly skilled and professional workers in technical and construction sectors, and were asked to apply following due procedure.

headline_en: 17 thousand workers could not go to Malaysia even with final clearance
summary_en: When Malaysia's labour market closed on 1 June 2024, 16,970 Bangladeshi workers who held final BMET clearance had not been able to go, some for lack of air tickets and some because employers never confirmed airport pickup. The ministry formed a six-member probe committee, said agencies must refund them, and workers can complain if charged above the government-fixed BDT 78,990. The article explains the 100-agency syndicate, the average 5.5 lakh taka workers paid, and the role of Bestinet and Amin Nur.

facts.statement: Recruiting agencies took BMET clearance for 493,642 workers for Malaysia, of whom 476,672 went; 16,970 workers with final clearance could not go before the 31 May 2024 deadline.

Of the 16,970 cleared workers who could not go to Malaysia, one part could not get air tickets and another part did not get the employer's final consent from Malaysia: the employer did not send assurance that it would receive them at the airport.

Malaysia's labour market closed from 1 June 2024; for now no new workers can go. The last date for workers to enter was 31 May 2024; Bangladesh's ministry had asked Malaysia about a week earlier to extend it by a week and got no response.

The government-fixed maximum cost per worker for going to Malaysia was BDT 78,990, but workers had to pay 5.5 lakh taka on average; a worker charged more than BDT 78,990 can report it to the ministry's probe committee.

The expatriates' welfare ministry formed a six-member probe committee headed by additional secretary (employment) Noor Md Mahbubul Haque to find corruption and irregularities in the Malaysia labour market and punish those responsible, to report within seven working days; it is also to work on compensation for affected workers, and anyone may file a complaint with it.

Ministry secretary Md Ruhul Amin said recruiting agencies will refund the workers who got clearance but could not go to Malaysia, BAIRA has taken responsibility for this, and legal action will be taken if money is not returned. He said no permission was given to send workers in the name of companies blacklisted by Malaysia.
facts.source_in_article: Md Ruhul Amin, secretary, expatriates' welfare ministry

facts.statement: Asked about workers finding no work in Malaysia, secretary Md Ruhul Amin said employers come to the Malaysian airport to receive workers, no case of a worker not being collected had occurred in the last few months, and work was being arranged for the 5,000 workers who earlier got no work.

The state minister said 23 special flights were arranged, after talks with the civil aviation ministry and Bangladesh Biman's top officials, to secure air tickets for Malaysia-bound workers, and that clearances were given whenever requested; he said the ministry was not negligent.

After Malaysia's market reopened in 2022 following a four-year closure, a group formed a syndicate of 100 agencies. Malaysia takes workers from 14 countries including Bangladesh and lets all agencies of the other countries send workers, but approves only specific agencies for Bangladesh, with no fixed criteria for choosing them.

The article says Bestinet, owner of 'Migram', the software of Malaysia's Foreign Workers Centralized Management System (FWCMS), took advantage of the agency-selection system; it is owned by Bangladeshi-origin Malaysian citizen Aminul Islam bin Abdul Nur, known as Amin Nur, who controls the whole worker-sending business from Malaysia.

People concerned say Bestinet's contract with the Malaysian government expired on 31 May 2024 and Malaysia stopped taking workers so as not to renew with the controversial company, but the contract may now be extended by three years, which could bring a new syndicate when the market reopens.

Allegations have been raised of syndicate irregularities and business worth thousands of crores of taka in sending workers to Malaysia, with four members of parliament linked; many workers got no work after arriving, and pressure from the UN and other international bodies led Malaysia to close the market saying it would redesign foreign worker recruitment.

The state minister said: 'I don't believe in syndicates. If the receiving country wants to take workers through its preferred recruiting agencies, that is its matter'; he gave no specific answer when asked whether Malaysia would again be allowed to pick agencies.

headline_en: 'Father, when will you send the money? They don't even give me food'
summary_en: Shakil Mia (24) of Saltha, Faridpur paid broker Mukul Thakur 12 lakh taka to reach Italy and was instead taken to Libya, where a trafficking ring is torturing him and demanding 15 lakh taka ransom with a death threat if unpaid by 26 March 2024. The family has no money left; the broker is reported to be in Italy; local officials say they will act if the family complains.

facts.statement: Shakil Mia's father Titul Mia, a poor farmer of Ramkantapur village, Saltha upazila, Faridpur, raised 12 lakh taka by borrowing, mortgaging land and taking high-interest loans and handed it to neighbour and broker Mukul Thakur, who promised to send Shakil to Italy.
Shakil Mia's sister Brishti Akter said he was taken first to India on 4 January 2024, then via Dubai to Libya; the family says he reached Libya on 14 January 2024.

In Libya the ring tortures Shakil daily, withholds food, phones the family so they hear the torture, and demands 15 lakh taka ransom, threatening to kill him if it is not paid by 26 March 2024. The sister says the torturers are Bangladeshis speaking Bangla and that the torture had been going on for 12 days (the article also says torture began after he arrived on 14 January).

Mukul Thakur of Ramkantapur village, Saltha, Faridpur, described as a member of a trafficking ring, came home some time ago and lured youths with going to Italy via Libya and high-paid jobs. His house was found locked; neighbour Kader Matubbar said Mukul is now in Italy and told him by Imo on Sunday night (about 24 March 2024) that Shakil is held by 'mafia' in Libya and he is trying to free him.

headline_en: 'My son didn't need to go to Italy; give him back to me'
summary_en: Three young men from Madaripur died when an overloaded engine boat carrying about 70 migrants from Libya towards Italy sank in Tunisian waters on Thursday 15 February 2024; Tunisia's coast guard rescued 52 alive and recovered 9 bodies. Families name a broker ring led by Mosharraf Kazi of Muksudpur, Gopalganj, which took 10 to 12 lakh taka from each youth. Police said no written complaint had been filed.

facts.statement: On Thursday 15 February 2024 an engine boat carrying about 70 migrants of various countries including Bangladeshis towards Italy sank after its bottom split on entering Tunisian waters in the Mediterranean; Tunisia's coast guard rescued 52 alive and recovered 9 dead, and several were missing. Three of the dead were from Madaripur: Md Samrat Bepari (23) of Paschim Panchkhola, Madaripur Sadar; Mamun Sheikh (22) of Paschim Swarmangal, Khalia union, Rajoir; and Sajal Bairagi (24) of Sendia village, Khalia union, Rajoir.

Mamun Sheikh, Sajal Bairagi and several others left home on 14 January 2024; Samrat Bepari had left eight months earlier through a local broker but could not enter Italy. They went from Bangladesh to Dubai for a few days, then to Benghazi, Libya, and were put on the boat for Italy on 15 February 2024.
The broker ring took 10 to 12 lakh taka from each youth from various areas of Madaripur on the promise of sending them to Italy.

Relatives say the ring's head is Mosharraf Kazi of Sundardi, Raghdi union, Muksudpur, Gopalganj, with associates Jubaraj Kazi of the same area and Russel Khan of Panchkhola, Madaripur Sadar. Mosharraf's phone was off when the reporter called repeatedly.

Mamun's brother Sajib Sheikh said the boat had about 70 people aboard though its capacity was 30 at most, and the overloading split its bottom. Sajal's father said his son had told him their 'game' (the crossing from Libya towards Italy) was about to happen and there would be no trouble.
Samrat's brother Azgar Bepari said the broker phoned to say his brother had died, and said he would bring the body home at his own responsibility and pay compensation.

Madaripur Additional SP Alaul Hasan said the families had filed no written complaint so far, but police operations against the broker ring were under way and legal action would follow once evidence was in hand.
